title: Egg (oocyte) quality & oxidative stress
summary: Egg quality depends above all on age: chromosome errors driven by cohesin loss and declining mitochondrial function rise steeply after the mid-30s, and no lifestyle change or supplement has been shown to reverse that in humans. Within that limit, the biggest controllable factors are not smoking, avoiding obesity and heavy drinking, taking folic acid, and eating a Mediterranean-style diet in the ~3 months of follicle growth before conception or IVF. Antioxidant supplements, including CoQ10 and melatonin, have at best low-quality evidence for women, and ESHRE does not recommend antioxidant therapy in IVF.

factors.name: Female age (oocyte ageing)
factors.headline: Age is by far the dominant, non-modifiable driver of egg quality: fecundity falls from about 32 and faster after 37, and the share of women with no chromosomally normal embryo rises from 2-6% (age 26-37) to 33% at 42 and 53% at 44.

dose.effective: Not modifiable. The practical lever is time: ACOG/ASRM advise expedited evaluation after 6 months of trying from age 35, and immediate evaluation over 40.
dose.studied_range: Aneuploidy data from embryos of women aged ~22-47; egg chromosome-segregation data from ages 9-43.
dose.timeframe: Gradual decline from the early 30s, steep after ~37; no lifestyle change reverses it.
dose.notes: Lifestyle can avoid adding damage on top of age, but no diet or supplement has been shown to restore the chromosomal quality of older eggs in humans. Egg freezing at a younger age and IVF with PGT-A or donor eggs are the only interventions that address age directly.

factors.mechanism: Eggs are arrested in meiosis for decades. Cohesin that holds sister chromatids together is laid down before birth and is not renewed, so it erodes with age, causing chromosome mis-segregation (aneuploidy). In parallel, oocyte mitochondria become less efficient (less ATP, more mtDNA instability), CoQ10-synthesis enzymes and NAD+ levels decline (animal data), and spindle assembly becomes error-prone.
factors.interactions: Age magnifies almost every other harm: [egg-smoking] and [egg-obesity] effects are layered on a declining baseline. Diet associations such as [egg-mediterranean-diet] were seen only in women under 35 in one cohort. Supplements aimed at mitochondria ([egg-coq10], [egg-nmn-nad]) target the age mechanism but have no human live-birth proof.
factors.caveats: Aneuploidy also rises slightly in the very young (U-curve), but this is a minor effect compared with the rise after the mid-30s. Ovarian reserve tests (AMH, antral follicle count) predict egg number and response to stimulation, not egg quality; a woman with high AMH at 42 still has age-typical aneuploidy rates. Claims that any supplement 'reverses egg ageing' are not supported by human data.

factors.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
factors.headline: PCOS carries measurable systemic oxidative stress (malondialdehyde about 47% higher, glutathione about 50% lower than controls, independent of weight); fertility problems are mainly ovulatory, and IVF outcomes are worse when PCOS coexists with obesity.

dose.effective: Management per the 2023 international guideline: healthy lifestyle first, then evidence-based medical and fertility treatment. In overweight women, losing 5% or more of body weight improved insulin, SHBG and cycles in an early study.
dose.studied_range: Weight loss studies 5-22% of body weight; lifestyle RCTs mostly 3-12 months.
dose.timeframe: Metabolic and ovulatory improvement over 3-6 months of weight loss.
dose.notes: Insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism, not oocytes per se, drive most of the problem; egg quality in lean, ovulating PCOS is often normal.

factors.mechanism: Hyperinsulinaemia and hyperandrogenism alter the follicular environment; chronic low-grade inflammation and lower antioxidant reserve (glutathione, paraoxonase-1) increase lipid peroxidation. Obesity adds lipotoxicity and further insulin resistance.
factors.interactions: Strongly interacts with [egg-obesity] and [egg-diabetes-insulin-resistance]; supplements studied mainly in PCOS: [egg-myo-inositol], [egg-nac]. Weight loss is covered by [egg-weight-loss].
factors.caveats: Raised oxidative markers in blood do not prove oxidative damage to eggs is the cause of infertility in PCOS; most infertility is anovulation, which is treatable. Lifestyle RCTs in PCOS have not reported live birth (Cochrane 2019 found none).

factors.name: Endometriosis
factors.headline: Endometriosis is an inflammatory, pro-oxidant condition linked to fewer and less mature eggs and lower oocyte mitochondrial content, but women with endometrioma have similar IVF live birth rates (OR 0.98) once eggs are retrieved.

dose.effective: Specialist management; surgery for endometrioma before IVF did not improve live birth (OR 0.90) and may reduce ovarian reserve.
dose.notes: Discuss fertility preservation and surgery timing with a reproductive specialist.

factors.mechanism: Peritoneal and follicular inflammation, iron from repeated bleeding (free-iron Fenton chemistry) and granulosa-cell ROS impair follicle development and oocyte maturation.
factors.interactions: Antioxidant supplements have been tried, but none has convincing live-birth data ([egg-antioxidant-supplements]).
factors.caveats: Evidence on egg quality is mostly from small biological studies; the main clinical effect is fewer oocytes and more cancelled cycles rather than lower live birth per transfer.

factors.name: Diabetes and insulin resistance
factors.headline: Women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes have 24-36% lower fecundability; in mice, maternal diabetes damages oocyte mitochondria and raises egg aneuploidy.

dose.effective: Good glycaemic control before conception (managed with the diabetes team); weight loss and physical activity for insulin resistance.
dose.timeframe: Preconception optimisation over at least 3 months covers one full cycle of follicle growth.
dose.notes: Preconception glucose control is also critical for reducing birth-defect risk.

factors.mechanism: Hyperglycaemia increases mitochondrial superoxide and advanced glycation end-products; in diabetic mice oocytes show abnormal mitochondrial structure, lower ATP and TCA metabolites, spindle defects and aneuploidy, and the defective mitochondria are passed to the embryo.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [egg-obesity] and [egg-pcos].
factors.caveats: Oocyte mechanism data are from animals; human data are fecundability associations.

factors.name: Obesity (BMI 30 or higher)
factors.headline: Obesity (BMI >= 30) is associated with about 15% lower IVF live birth (RR 0.85), worse with PCOS, and with an inflamed, lipid-rich follicular environment.

dose.effective: Aim for BMI under 30 and ideally 18.5-24.9; in PCOS, even 5% weight loss improved hormones and cycles.
dose.studied_range: BMI categories 18.5-24.9 vs >= 30 kg/m2 in meta-analysis.
dose.too_much: Underweight (BMI < 18.5) and very low energy availability also impair ovulation (see [egg-vigorous-exercise-red-s]).
dose.timeframe: Follicular environment reflects the preceding ~3 months.
dose.notes: Donor-egg data did not change the overall conclusion, suggesting both egg and uterine effects.

factors.mechanism: Higher follicular fluid insulin, triglycerides, lactate and CRP; lipid accumulation in oocytes causes ER stress, reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and cumulus-cell apoptosis (lipotoxicity).
factors.interactions: Compounds [egg-pcos] and [egg-diabetes-insulin-resistance]. Weight-loss evidence is in [egg-weight-loss]. Vigorous exercise was not harmful in women with BMI >= 25 ([egg-moderate-exercise]).
factors.caveats: Associations are confounded by PCOS and metabolic disease. Weight-loss RCTs before IVF have not raised IVF live birth (see [egg-weight-loss]).

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, BMI >= 30 vs normal

factors.name: Chemotherapy and pelvic radiation
factors.headline: Gonadotoxic chemotherapy and ovarian radiation destroy the egg reserve directly; less than 2 Gy is estimated to kill half of human oocytes.

dose.effective: Fertility-preservation counselling before treatment; egg or embryo freezing is standard care.
dose.too_much: Oocyte LD50 estimated at < 2 Gy; chemotherapy risk depends on drug (e.g. cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin), cumulative dose and age.
dose.timeframe: Primordial-follicle oocytes die within 12-24 h of gonadotoxic drug exposure, so preservation must happen before treatment.
dose.notes: GnRH agonists may be offered (e.g. breast cancer) but are not a substitute for proven preservation methods.

factors.mechanism: DNA double-strand breaks in primordial-follicle oocytes trigger apoptosis; radiation generates ROS and direct DNA damage.
factors.interactions: No antioxidant has been shown to protect human ovaries from chemotherapy.
factors.caveats: This is a medical-referral factor, not a lifestyle one.

factors.name: Cigarette smoking
factors.headline: Smoking is the largest avoidable toxic exposure for eggs: about 60% higher odds of infertility, roughly halved odds of IVF live birth (OR 0.54), lower AMH and twice the risk of early menopause.

dose.effective: Zero. Risk is dose-dependent (cigarettes/day, years smoked, pack-years).
dose.studied_range: Current vs never smokers; dose-response up to >20 cigarettes/day and 15-20+ years.
dose.too_much: Any active smoking. 11-15 pack-years: ~4-fold risk of premature menopause; 15-20 years' duration: much higher.
dose.timeframe: Quitting at least 3 months before trying covers one follicle-growth cycle; menopause-timing risk normalises about 10 years after quitting.
dose.notes: ASRM's 2024 opinion also reviews nicotine and marijuana as potential reproductive harms.

factors.mechanism: Tobacco smoke delivers polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, cadmium and other oxidants that accelerate follicle loss (lower AMH), raise follicular oxidative stress and impair oocyte maturation.
factors.interactions: Adds to [egg-maternal-age]. Cadmium overlaps with [egg-heavy-metals]. Cessation is covered by [egg-smoking-cessation].
factors.caveats: Evidence is observational, but consistent across designs and dose-dependent, which supports causation.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth per cycle, smokers

factors.name: Stopping smoking
factors.headline: Quitting removes the biggest avoidable egg toxin; former smokers' excess menopause risk is much smaller than current smokers' and disappears about 10 years after quitting.

dose.effective: Complete cessation, ideally at least 3 months before trying or before IVF stimulation.
dose.studied_range: Former vs current smokers, years since quitting.
dose.timeframe: One follicle-growth cycle (~3 months) for the follicular environment; longer for ovarian-reserve effects.
dose.notes: Lost follicles are not regained, so earlier is better. Use evidence-based cessation support.

factors.mechanism: Removes the exogenous oxidant and toxicant load (PAHs, cadmium) on growing follicles.
factors.interactions: See [egg-smoking].
factors.caveats: No RCT has randomised women to quit and measured egg quality; the benefit is inferred from the dose-response and former-smoker data.

factors.name: Alcohol
factors.headline: Heavier drinking lowers fertility, but under about 7 drinks a week effects on conception are small or undetectable; one IVF cohort saw 16% lower live birth at 4 or more drinks a week.

dose.effective: Ideally none while trying; if drinking, keep well under 4 drinks/week before and during IVF.
dose.studied_range: 0 to >= 14 servings/week; light <= 12.5 g ethanol/day vs >12.5 g/day.
dose.too_much: >= 4 drinks/week associated with lower IVF live birth (OR 0.84); >12.5 g/day (about one drink/day) with ~23% lower fecundability; ASRM: >2 drinks/day best avoided.
dose.timeframe: Preconception months; stop entirely once pregnancy is possible (fetal safety).
dose.notes: Data do not separate binge from regular drinking; binge drinking in the fertile window is probably worse.

factors.mechanism: Ethanol metabolism generates acetaldehyde and ROS (CYP2E1), disturbs estrogen and LH signalling, and depletes antioxidant reserves.
factors.interactions: Effects combine across partners in IVF (both drinking >= 4/week: OR 0.79).
factors.caveats: Studies conflict: a large Danish cohort found no effect below 14/week, and the EARTH IVF cohort found no effect of <= 12 g/day. The pregnancy-safety case for abstinence is stronger than the egg-quality case.

factors.name: Caffeine (high intake)
factors.headline: Moderate caffeine (under ~200 mg/day) shows little or no effect on conceiving or IVF success; the clearer risk is miscarriage once pregnant, rising about 7% per 100 mg/day.

dose.effective: Keep under 200 mg/day (about 1-2 cups of brewed coffee) while trying and in pregnancy.
dose.studied_range: <50 to >700 mg/day.
dose.too_much: > 500 mg/day linked to lower fertility (ASRM); in pregnancy, 350-699 mg/day RR 1.40 and >= 700 mg/day RR 1.72 for pregnancy loss.
dose.timeframe: Matters most from conception onward.
dose.notes: Keep fertility and miscarriage data separate: preconception intake was not associated with miscarriage in a large Danish cohort; early-pregnancy intake was.

factors.mechanism: Adenosine-receptor antagonism; effects on ovulation and tubal function are speculative. Not primarily an oxidative-stress factor.
factors.interactions: Coffee and tea are also polyphenol sources; there is no evidence that this offsets or adds to the caffeine effect on fertility. For general (non-pregnancy) oxidative-stress effects of coffee, see [coffee].
factors.caveats: Observational and confounded by pregnancy nausea (women with healthier pregnancies feel sick and drink less coffee). Male caffeine intake >= 300 mg/day was associated with lower fecundability in one cohort.

key_numbers.label: Miscarriage risk per +100 mg/day in pregnancy

factors.name: Air pollution (NO2, fine particles)
factors.headline: Higher traffic-related NO2 exposure is associated with lower AMH and lower IVF live birth (e.g. OR 0.76 per 0.01 ppm after embryo transfer); effect sizes per person are modest and hard to separate from other urban factors.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure where practical: avoid exercising beside heavy traffic, use HEPA filtration indoors on high-pollution days.
dose.studied_range: Residential and IVF-lab NO2, ozone, PM2.5 and PM10 from monitoring models.
dose.too_much: No safe threshold established; associations were per 0.01 ppm (Legro) or 20 ppb (Gaskins) increase in NO2.
dose.timeframe: Exposure in the ~3 months before IVF was studied.
dose.notes: In one IVF cohort the NO2-live birth association was absent in women taking >= 800 ug/day supplemental folate (hypothesis-generating).

factors.mechanism: Inhaled particles and NO2 cause systemic inflammation and oxidative stress; PAHs adsorbed on particles are ovotoxic.
factors.interactions: Possible modification by [egg-folic-acid]. Overlaps with [egg-smoking] (shared PAH exposure).
factors.caveats: All observational, with exposure estimated from home address. Individual control is limited; do not let this become a source of anxiety.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth per +0.01 ppm NO2 (post-transfer)

factors.name: Phthalates (DEHP and related plasticizers)
factors.headline: In the EARTH IVF cohort, women in the top quartile of urinary DEHP metabolites had fewer eggs and about 19 percentage points lower live birth per cycle than the bottom quartile.

dose.effective: Lower exposure: eat more fresh, less ultra-processed and packaged food; avoid heating food in plastic; choose fragrance-free personal-care products.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of urinary phthalate metabolites (spot urine samples).
dose.too_much: No established threshold; risk scaled with quartile.
dose.timeframe: Urinary levels vary day to day, reflecting recent exposure; follicles develop over ~3 months, so reduce exposure across that window.
dose.notes: Single EARTH cohort with 256 women; replication is limited.

factors.mechanism: Anti-androgenic and endocrine-disrupting effects on granulosa-cell steroidogenesis; animal studies show follicular oxidative stress and atresia.
factors.interactions: Often co-occurs with [egg-bpa] exposure from packaged food.
factors.caveats: Urine levels fluctuate day to day, so single samples misclassify exposure; confounding by diet quality is possible.

key_numbers.label: Live birth difference, top vs bottom DEHP quartile

factors.name: Bisphenol A (BPA)
factors.headline: Each log-unit increase in urinary BPA was associated with 12% fewer eggs retrieved in IVF; BPA causes egg aneuploidy in animals, but human outcome data are small and inconsistent.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure: fewer canned foods, avoid polycarbonate containers and heating food in plastic, minimise thermal-paper receipts.
dose.studied_range: Urinary BPA < 0.4 to 25.5 ug/L.
dose.timeframe: Reduce exposure across the ~3-month follicle-growth window.
dose.notes: Human data come from small IVF cohorts at one clinic.

factors.mechanism: Estrogen-receptor activity; in animals disrupts meiotic spindle formation and steroidogenesis and increases oxidative stress.
factors.interactions: [egg-phthalates] come from similar sources.
factors.caveats: Small cohorts (84 women); human evidence is not strong enough to quantify live-birth effects.

key_numbers.label: Oocytes retrieved per log-unit urinary BPA

factors.name: Heavy metals (mercury, lead, cadmium)
factors.headline: Higher follicular-fluid mercury (above ~0.5 ug/L) and lead were associated with lower IVF live birth (lead RR 0.68) in a small study; cadmium exposure comes mainly from smoking.

dose.effective: Favour smaller, lower-mercury fish over large predatory fish (e.g. shark, swordfish); do not smoke (main cadmium source).
dose.studied_range: Follicular fluid Hg, Pb, Cd, As in 56 IVF patients.
dose.too_much: Follicular fluid Hg > ~0.51 ug/L associated with lower biochemical pregnancy and live birth.
dose.notes: Keep eating fish: the omega-3 benefit is real; choose low-mercury species.

factors.mechanism: Metals bind thiol groups, deplete glutathione and inactivate antioxidant enzymes; cadmium and lead can displace essential metals and promote Fenton-type ROS generation.
factors.interactions: Trades off against [egg-omega-3] (fish is the main source of both); [egg-smoking] supplies cadmium.
factors.caveats: One small cohort; associations were non-linear and imprecise.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, higher follicular lead

factors.name: Very intense exercise and low energy availability (RED-S)
factors.headline: In lean women, 5 or more hours a week of vigorous exercise was associated with about 32% lower monthly chance of conception; exercising to exhaustion or on most days was linked to 2-3 times the odds of fertility problems.

dose.effective: If trying to conceive and lean, cap vigorous exercise below ~5 h/week and swap some for moderate activity; eat enough to keep regular cycles.
dose.studied_range: Vigorous activity 0 to >= 5 h/week (Danish cohort); frequency/intensity categories (Norwegian cohort).
dose.too_much: >= 5 h/week vigorous: FR 0.68 in lean women; exercising most days: 3.2-fold odds of fertility problems; exercising to exhaustion: 2.3-fold.
dose.timeframe: Cycle recovery after restoring energy balance can take months.
dose.notes: Missed or irregular periods in an active woman are a red flag for low energy availability (hypothalamic suppression).

factors.mechanism: Low energy availability suppresses GnRH pulsatility (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea), lowering estrogen and ovulation; this is an energy-signalling problem more than an oxidative one.
factors.interactions: No adverse association in women with BMI >= 25, for whom activity helps ([egg-moderate-exercise], [egg-weight-loss]). Different from acute oxidative damage after ultra-endurance events ([overtraining-ultraendurance]); in general health, vigorous exercise in normal amounts is beneficial ([hiit-vigorous-exercise]).
factors.caveats: Observational and self-reported; vigorous exercise was not associated with worse IVF outcomes in the EARTH cohort.

factors.name: Moderate physical activity
factors.headline: Moderate activity (e.g. brisk walking, cycling) is linked to slightly higher fecundability (FR 1.18 at >= 5 h/week) and, in women with reproductive problems, exercise interventions roughly doubled pregnancy rates in small trials.

dose.effective: Regular moderate activity; >= 5 h/week of moderate activity was associated with slightly higher fecundability, and any activity type helped women with BMI >= 25.
dose.studied_range: Moderate activity < 1 to >= 5 h/week; intervention trials mainly in PCOS and obesity.
dose.too_much: See [egg-vigorous-exercise-red-s]: >= 5 h/week vigorous activity in lean women.
dose.timeframe: Insulin sensitivity improves within weeks; ovulatory changes over months.
dose.notes: Pre-IVF activity (median 2.8 h/week moderate-to-vigorous) was not harmful.

factors.mechanism: Improves insulin sensitivity and reduces inflammation; regular moderate exercise up-regulates endogenous antioxidant defenses (hormesis).
factors.interactions: Combines with [egg-weight-loss] in overweight women.
factors.caveats: Intervention trials are few and small; the benefit is clearest in women with PCOS or overweight.

key_numbers.label: Pregnancy, PA intervention vs no therapy

factors.name: Poor sleep and circadian disruption
factors.headline: Frequent trouble sleeping was associated with about 13% lower monthly chance of conception; shift work is linked to menstrual disruption and night shifts to early miscarriage, but not clearly to infertility.

dose.effective: Aim for 7-9 h/night with a regular schedule; treat insomnia and sleep apnea.
dose.studied_range: Sleep < 6 to >= 9 h/day; shift vs day work.
dose.too_much: Trouble sleeping > 50% of nights: FR 0.87; night shifts: aOR 1.41 for early pregnancy loss.
dose.notes: Melatonin supplements are discussed separately ([egg-melatonin]); they are not a substitute for sleep.

factors.mechanism: Ovarian and pituitary clocks regulate the LH surge; circadian disruption alters melatonin (a follicular antioxidant), cortisol and insulin sensitivity.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [egg-psychological-stress]. The shift-work findings also apply to [shift-work-circadian].
factors.caveats: Observational and confounded by depression and stress; shift work-infertility association lost significance after adjustment.

key_numbers.label: Fecundability, trouble sleeping > 50% of the time

factors.name: Psychological stress
factors.headline: A high salivary alpha-amylase stress marker was linked to 29% lower fecundability in one cohort, but a meta-analysis of 3583 IVF patients found pre-treatment anxiety or depression did not affect pregnancy rates.

dose.effective: Stress management for wellbeing (counselling, CBT, mindfulness, exercise); not proven to raise pregnancy rates.
dose.notes: Reassure people that stress caused by infertility does not ruin their IVF chances.

factors.mechanism: Sympathetic and HPA-axis activation can suppress GnRH/LH and raise systemic oxidative stress, but direct evidence of oocyte damage in humans is lacking.
factors.interactions: Linked with [egg-sleep-circadian].
factors.caveats: Reverse causation (infertility causes stress) is likely in many studies; avoid blaming patients.

factors.name: Mediterranean-style diet
factors.headline: Women in the lowest third of Mediterranean-diet adherence had much lower IVF live birth (26.6% vs 48.8%) in a Greek cohort of women under 35, but pooled evidence is inconsistent and no RCT has tested it.

dose.effective: Daily vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, olive oil and nuts; fish 2+ times/week; little processed meat, sweets and refined snacks.
dose.studied_range: MedDietScore 0-55 (tertiles <= 30 vs >= 36); EARTH quartiles.
dose.timeframe: Adopt at least 3 months before trying or IVF.
dose.notes: In the US EARTH cohort, benefit plateaued after the second quartile: the gain comes from avoiding a poor diet rather than perfect adherence.

factors.mechanism: Supplies folate, vitamin B6, omega-3 and polyphenols, lowers homocysteine and systemic inflammation, and improves insulin sensitivity; higher blood and follicular-fluid folate/B6 were seen with this pattern.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [egg-profertility-diet], [egg-folic-acid] and [egg-omega-3]; also supports [egg-weight-loss].
factors.caveats: All observational; association seen only in women under 35 in one study and no association with oocyte yield or embryo quality. A 2023 meta-analysis judged the evidence insufficient for clinical application.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, lowest vs highest tertile

factors.name: "Profertility" diet pattern (EARTH study)
factors.headline: A pattern of supplemental folic acid, B12 and vitamin D plus low-pesticide produce, whole grains, dairy, soy and seafood was associated with 53% higher odds of IVF live birth per SD of adherence (top vs bottom quartile: +28 percentage points).

dose.effective: Folic acid supplement (>= 400-800 ug/day), adequate B12 and vitamin D, whole grains, dairy, soy foods, seafood instead of other meats, and lower-pesticide-residue fruit and vegetables.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of a score from a validated food-frequency questionnaire.
dose.timeframe: Diet in the year before treatment was measured.
dose.notes: Not related to estradiol, oocyte counts or endometrial thickness; associated with less clinical pregnancy loss.

factors.mechanism: Likely via one-carbon metabolism (folate/B12), vitamin D signalling and lower pesticide exposure rather than a direct antioxidant effect.
factors.interactions: Contains [egg-folic-acid] and [egg-vitamin-d]; overlaps with [egg-mediterranean-diet] and [egg-omega-3].
factors.caveats: Derived and tested in the same single US cohort (357 women) by the same group, which risks overfitting; needs independent replication or an RCT.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth odds per SD adherence
Live birth, top vs bottom quartile

factors.name: Folic acid / folate
factors.headline: Folic acid is mandatory preconception care (400-800 ug/day prevents neural tube defects) and is also consistently associated with better fertility: 15% higher fecundability and 20 percentage points higher IVF live birth at > 800 ug/day supplemental folate.

dose.effective: 400-800 ug/day folic acid, started before conception (ideally 3 months ahead) and continued through early pregnancy.
dose.studied_range: Supplemental folate < 400 to > 800 ug/day (cohorts).
dose.too_much: Higher doses only on a clinician's advice for specific indications.
dose.timeframe: Before conception for neural tube protection; 3 months covers follicle development.
dose.notes: Usually taken as a prenatal multivitamin. Diet folate (leafy greens, legumes) is good but does not replace the supplement.

factors.mechanism: Folate supports one-carbon metabolism: DNA synthesis and repair, methylation and homocysteine clearance. Elevated homocysteine in follicular fluid is linked to poorer embryo quality.
factors.interactions: Core of [egg-profertility-diet]; may buffer the [egg-air-pollution] association in one cohort.
factors.caveats: Fertility benefits are observational; the neural-tube benefit is RCT-proven and reason enough to take it.

factors.name: Vitamin D (correcting deficiency)
factors.headline: Vitamin D-replete women had about 33% higher odds of IVF live birth than deficient women, but RCTs of supplementation in deficient women improved only chemical pregnancy, not clinical pregnancy.

dose.effective: Test 25(OH)D and correct deficiency with a clinician; there is no evidence that extra vitamin D helps women who are already replete.
dose.studied_range: Observational: replete vs deficient/insufficient 25(OH)D; 5 RCTs of supplementation in deficient women.
dose.too_much: Avoid unsupervised megadoses.
dose.timeframe: Correct deficiency before IVF or trying, within the 3-month preparation window.
dose.notes: Benefit, if any, is limited to correcting deficiency.

factors.mechanism: Vitamin D receptors are present in granulosa cells and endometrium; vitamin D influences AMH signalling and immune tolerance.
factors.interactions: Part of [egg-profertility-diet].
factors.caveats: Observational links are confounded by overall health, BMI and outdoor activity; RCT evidence is small.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, replete vs deficient

factors.name: Omega-3 fats (EPA/DHA from fish)
factors.headline: Each 1% higher serum long-chain omega-3 was associated with 8% higher probability of IVF live birth; in mice omega-3-rich diets preserved egg quality into older age.

dose.effective: Eat lower-mercury fatty fish regularly as part of the diet; studies measured serum levels and dietary share rather than a fixed supplement dose (replacing 1% of energy from saturated fat with long-chain omega-3 was associated with RR 2.37 for live birth).
dose.studied_range: Serum omega-3 4.7% median (IQR 3.8-5.8%) of total fatty acids.
dose.too_much: High-mercury fish (see [egg-heavy-metals]).
dose.timeframe: Adopt within the 3-month preconception window.
dose.notes: Human evidence is from observational IVF cohorts; no adequate RCT on live birth.

factors.mechanism: Incorporation into membranes, anti-inflammatory lipid mediators, possible effects on follicular steroidogenesis.
factors.interactions: Trade-off with [egg-heavy-metals]; part of [egg-mediterranean-diet] and [egg-profertility-diet].
factors.caveats: Small cohort (100 women); mouse data on reproductive ageing have not been replicated in humans.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth probability per +1% serum LC omega-3

factors.name: Weight loss when overweight or obese
factors.headline: In overweight and obese women, diet-plus-exercise programmes increased natural pregnancy (RR 1.59) and ovulation, but two RCTs (LIFEstyle, Nordic trial) found that delaying fertility treatment for weight loss did not improve live birth from treatment.

dose.effective: 5-10% of body weight via a reduced-calorie diet plus aerobic exercise; >5% loss improved insulin and cycles in PCOS.
dose.studied_range: Mean losses 4.4 kg (LIFEstyle, 6 months) to 9.4 kg (12 weeks of 880 kcal/day low-calorie diet).
dose.too_much: Do not delay treatment for long in women over ~35: time lost costs egg quality ([egg-maternal-age]).
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Weight loss increased spontaneous conceptions (10.5% vs 2.6% in the Nordic trial). Best for women not yet in IVF or with anovulation.

factors.mechanism: Lowers insulin and free androgens, raises SHBG, reduces follicular lipid and inflammatory load (lipotoxicity).
factors.interactions: Works with [egg-moderate-exercise] and [egg-mediterranean-diet]; counteracts [egg-obesity] and [egg-pcos].
factors.caveats: LIFEstyle: 27.1% vs 35.2% healthy term singleton births, favouring prompt treatment, partly because the intervention arm delayed treatment by 6 months. Weight loss is still worthwhile for pregnancy health.
