factors.name: Antioxidant supplements in general (for the female partner)
factors.headline: The Cochrane review of 63 trials found only low- to very-low-quality evidence that antioxidants help subfertile women, several included trials have since been retracted, and ESHRE does not recommend antioxidant therapy in IVF.

dose.effective: No antioxidant product or dose is proven to raise live birth in women.
dose.studied_range: Trials of NAC, melatonin, L-arginine, myo-inositol, carnitine, selenium, vitamins C/E/D, B complex, CoQ10 and omega-3, usually for 1-3 cycles.
dose.too_much: No clear harms in pooled data (miscarriage OR 1.13, GI effects OR 1.55, both NS), but in animals blocking ROS impairs ovulation, so more is not better.
dose.timeframe: Trials typically 1-3 months.
dose.notes: Cochrane's headline OR for live birth (1.81) rests on very-low-quality, small, often unregistered trials; treat it as unreliable. A 2026 editorial note lists 7 retracted and 2 'concern' trials in the review.

factors.mechanism: Direct scavengers cannot reach the mitochondrial sites where oocyte ROS are generated at meaningful concentrations, and ROS are required for LH-triggered ovulation; the 'antioxidant paradox' applies.
factors.interactions: Specific agents are listed separately: [egg-coq10], [egg-melatonin], [egg-myo-inositol], [egg-nac], [egg-vitamin-e-c], [egg-l-carnitine], [egg-alpha-lipoic-acid], [egg-resveratrol], [egg-nmn-nad]. Antioxidants for the male partner are a different question.
factors.caveats: Supplement marketing for 'egg quality' far outruns the evidence. Spending on lifestyle basics and folic acid is better supported.

key_numbers.label: Live birth, antioxidants vs control (very low quality)

factors.name: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol)
factors.headline: The best-studied 'egg quality' supplement: 600 mg/day for 60 days before IVF increased eggs retrieved (median 4 vs 2) and good embryos in young poor responders, and meta-analyses show higher clinical pregnancy (OR ~2.2-2.4) but no significant live-birth gain.

dose.effective: 600 mg/day (200 mg three times daily) for 60 days before IVF (Xu 2018 RCT).
dose.studied_range: 600 mg/day in the Xu RCT; pooled RCTs (5 trials, 449 women) used varying regimens.
dose.too_much: No harms reported in these trials.
dose.timeframe: At least 2 months before stimulation; ideally covering the ~3-month follicle-growth window.
dose.notes: Fat-soluble. Evidence is mainly in poor responders/low ovarian reserve; no good data in women with normal reserve.

factors.mechanism: CoQ10 carries electrons in the mitochondrial respiratory chain and is a lipid-phase antioxidant. Ageing oocytes in mice and women express less of the CoQ-synthesis enzymes PDSS2 and COQ6; in mice CoQ10 restored oocyte mitochondrial function and reduced spindle defects.
factors.interactions: Mechanistically overlaps with [egg-nmn-nad] (both target mitochondrial ageing). Often bundled with [egg-melatonin] and [egg-myo-inositol] in commercial products, which prevents attributing effects.
factors.caveats: Small trials; the Xu RCT was open-label without placebo and excluded 17 non-compliant women. ESHRE does not recommend antioxidant therapy in IVF. Not shown to reduce aneuploidy in humans.

key_numbers.label: Cumulative live birth, CoQ10 vs control (NS)

factors.name: Melatonin
factors.headline: Melatonin is a natural follicular antioxidant; in IVF RCTs it raised clinical pregnancy (OR 1.43) and egg/embryo counts in pooled low-quality data, but not live birth (OR 1.38, NS), and a placebo-controlled dose trial saw no change in follicle numbers.

dose.effective: 3 mg/day at night during IVF stimulation was the dose used in the early Japanese studies; not proven.
dose.studied_range: 3 mg/day to 8 mg twice daily.
dose.too_much: Higher doses (up to 8 mg twice daily) did not add benefit; doses below and above showed no live-birth difference in Cochrane comparisons.
dose.timeframe: Usually from early follicular phase to egg retrieval.
dose.notes: Melatonin is a hormone with circadian effects; doses up to 8 mg twice daily did not cause daytime sleepiness in an IVF trial, but there is no reason to use high doses.

factors.mechanism: Concentrated in follicular fluid, scavenges hydroxyl radicals and stimulates antioxidant enzymes; follicular melatonin was inversely related to 8-OHdG oxidative DNA damage.
factors.interactions: Frequently combined with [egg-myo-inositol]; a large combination trial was retracted in 2026.
factors.caveats: Trials are heterogeneous (PCOS to poor responders), small and low quality; the key Tamura data were non-randomized.

factors.name: Myo-inositol (in PCOS)
factors.headline: Widely used in PCOS, but the Cochrane review rated the evidence very low quality and could not show a live-birth benefit (OR 2.42, 95% CI 0.75-7.83); the 2023 PCOS guideline review calls it limited and inconclusive.

dose.effective: Trials commonly used 4 g/day myo-inositol with 400 ug folic acid (e.g. the now-retracted Pacchiarotti trial); no dose is proven to raise live birth.
dose.studied_range: 11 of 13 Cochrane trials used myo-inositol as pre-treatment before IVF; 2 during ovulation induction.
dose.too_much: Mild GI effects; fewer GI effects than metformin.
dose.timeframe: Pre-treatment before IVF stimulation in most trials.
dose.notes: D-chiro-inositol may help ovulation per the guideline review, but evidence is very uncertain. One widely cited myo-inositol plus melatonin RCT (526 women) was retracted in 2026.

factors.mechanism: Inositol phosphoglycans act as second messengers for insulin and FSH signalling; may improve insulin sensitivity in PCOS.
factors.interactions: Alternative to or adjunct with metformin; often combined with [egg-melatonin] and [egg-folic-acid].
factors.caveats: Industry-linked trials, poor reporting and a retraction. Not relevant for women without PCOS.

key_numbers.label: Live birth, MI vs standard (2 RCTs)

factors.name: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) in PCOS
factors.headline: In PCOS, NAC added to clomiphene improved ovulation and pregnancy vs placebo in small, biased trials, but it was inferior to metformin and live-birth data are thin.

dose.effective: 1.2 g/day (with clomiphene in clomiphene-resistant PCOS) in the original RCT.
dose.studied_range: 1.2 g/day in the main RCT; 8 RCTs (910 women) pooled in meta-analysis.
dose.timeframe: During ovulation-induction cycles.
dose.notes: A glutathione precursor; available as a supplement in some countries and a drug in others.

factors.mechanism: Supplies cysteine for glutathione synthesis; may improve insulin sensitivity.
factors.interactions: Compared against metformin and [egg-l-carnitine] in trials; the NAC-vs-carnitine trial in the Cochrane review was flagged for integrity concerns.
factors.caveats: Many trials come from a few centres; high risk of selection, attrition and reporting bias. The 1.2 g/day trial's 49% vs 1% ovulation contrast is implausibly large.

key_numbers.label: Ovulation, NAC + clomiphene vs placebo + clomiphene

factors.name: DHEA in poor responders
factors.headline: Cochrane (2024, moderate certainty): DHEA probably makes little or no difference to live birth in poor responders (OR 1.30, NS); testosterone pre-treatment looks more promising (OR 2.53). ESHRE does not recommend DHEA.

dose.effective: Not recommended. A typical trial dose was 75 mg/day before and during the IVF cycle.
dose.studied_range: 75 mg/day (Wiser 2010) and similar regimens.
dose.too_much: Androgenic side effects (acne, hair growth); a hormone, use only under medical supervision.
dose.timeframe: Started before the IVF cycle and continued during stimulation in trials.
dose.notes: Network meta-analysis showed higher clinical pregnancy with DHEA (OR 2.46), but the larger Cochrane pooled analysis with live birth as outcome did not.

factors.mechanism: Androgen precursor proposed to increase FSH sensitivity of small antral follicles; not an antioxidant.
factors.interactions: Compare [egg-coq10] in the same poor-responder population.
factors.caveats: Early small trials (e.g. 33 women) overstated benefit.

factors.name: Vitamin E and vitamin C supplements
factors.headline: Vitamin E (600 mg/day) lowered follicular oxidative markers in a tiny study, and supplement use was associated with slightly shorter time to pregnancy in some subgroups, but there is no convincing RCT evidence of more live births.

dose.effective: Meet needs from food (nuts, seeds, vegetable oils, fruit, vegetables); routine high-dose supplements are not supported.
dose.studied_range: Vitamin E 600 mg/day (Tamura); vitamin C and E in mixed antioxidant trials in the Cochrane review.
dose.too_much: No benefit shown, so there is no reason to take high-dose supplements.
dose.notes: Typical prenatal vitamins already contain modest amounts.

factors.mechanism: Vitamin E is the main lipid-phase chain-breaking antioxidant; vitamin C regenerates it. Neither targets mitochondrial ROS production.
factors.interactions: Part of [egg-antioxidant-supplements].
factors.caveats: Classic antioxidant paradox: big mechanistic story, no clinical proof.

factors.name: L-carnitine / acetyl-L-carnitine
factors.headline: Evidence for women is weak; the most-cited positive RCT (L-carnitine 3 g/day in clomiphene-resistant PCOS) has been retracted.

dose.effective: No proven dose for female fertility.
dose.studied_range: 3 g/day in the retracted PCOS trial.
dose.notes: Male-factor evidence is separate and somewhat better.

factors.mechanism: Shuttles long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation, which oocytes use for energy.
factors.interactions: Included in [egg-antioxidant-supplements] analyses.
factors.caveats: Retraction of the main trial removes the main human evidence.

factors.name: Resveratrol
factors.headline: Resveratrol may improve some follicular markers (an 800 mg/day RCT in PCOS raised oocyte maturity without changing pregnancy rates), but it suppresses endometrial decidualization, and 200 mg/day during embryo-transfer cycles was associated with lower pregnancy (OR 0.54) and more miscarriage (OR 2.60).

dose.effective: Not recommended while trying to conceive or around embryo transfer.
dose.studied_range: 200 mg/day (retrospective IVF cohort); 800 mg/day for 60 days (PCOS RCT, 56 women).
dose.too_much: Any use in the luteal phase or early pregnancy (possible anti-implantation effect; teratogenicity not excluded).
dose.notes: A clear example where an 'anti-ageing' antioxidant may harm the uterus even if it helps the ovary.

factors.mechanism: SIRT1 activation and antioxidant effects in the ovary; in endometrium it down-regulates the CRABP2-RAR pathway, inhibiting decidualization needed for implantation.
factors.interactions: Sirtuin-pathway overlap with [egg-nmn-nad].
factors.caveats: Harm signal is retrospective; benefit signal is a single small RCT on surrogate outcomes.

key_numbers.label: Clinical pregnancy, resveratrol during transfer cycles

factors.name: NMN / NAD+ precursors (NMN, NR)
factors.headline: NAD+ falls in ageing mouse eggs and NMN restored egg quality and fertility in aged mice, but there are no human data on egg quality, pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: No human fertility dose exists; all egg data are from mice.
dose.studied_range: Animal studies only.
dose.too_much: Unknown in pregnancy; safety in early embryos not studied in humans.
dose.notes: Marketed heavily as 'egg rejuvenation'; this is extrapolation from mice.

factors.mechanism: Raises NAD+, a cofactor for sirtuins (e.g. SIRT2) and mitochondrial metabolism; in aged mice restored spindle assembly, mitochondrial function and lowered ROS.
factors.interactions: Shares the mitochondrial-ageing target with [egg-coq10]; sirtuin overlap with [egg-resveratrol].
factors.caveats: Mouse reproductive ageing differs from human (human egg aneuploidy is driven largely by cohesin loss over decades).

factors.name: Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA)
factors.headline: A systematic review reports some positive effects on oocyte maturation, embryo grade and endometriosis pain, but the trials are small and no live-birth benefit has been shown.

dose.effective: No proven dose for female fertility.
dose.studied_range: Small trials, often combined with inositol or other agents.
dose.notes: Mostly from Italian combination-product studies.

factors.mechanism: Mitochondrial enzyme cofactor and redox-cycling antioxidant that regenerates glutathione, vitamins C and E.
factors.interactions: Usually given with [egg-myo-inositol].
factors.caveats: Evidence base is too weak to recommend.

mechanisms.name: ROS as a required ovulation signal
mechanisms.description: A transient burst of reactive oxygen species after the LH surge is needed for cumulus expansion, progesterone production, EGF-receptor/MAPK signalling and follicle rupture. In mice, flooding the ovary with antioxidants reduced ovulation. Oxidative stress is harmful only when ROS are excessive or prolonged, which is one reason high-dose antioxidant supplements are not automatically helpful.

mechanisms.name: Oocyte mitochondria and maternally inherited mtDNA
mechanisms.description: The oocyte is the most mitochondria-rich cell in the body and its mitochondria supply the early embryo until embryonic mitochondrial biogenesis starts. mtDNA is inherited only from the mother (sperm mtDNA is eliminated) and passes through a genetic bottleneck, so oocyte mitochondrial quality matters for the next generation. With age, oocyte mitochondria produce less ATP, mtDNA becomes less stable and CoQ10-synthesis enzymes decline.

mechanisms.name: Cohesin loss and egg aneuploidy
mechanisms.description: Eggs pause in meiosis I from before birth until ovulation. The cohesin complexes that hold chromosome pairs together are not replaced, so they erode over decades; in older women this centromeric cohesion loss drives chromosome mis-segregation, giving a U-shaped aneuploidy curve with a steep rise after the mid-30s. This is the main reason age dominates egg quality, and it is not an oxidative process that antioxidants are known to fix.

mechanisms.name: Declining NAD+ in ageing oocytes
mechanisms.description: In mice, oocyte NAD+ falls with age; restoring it with NMN improved mitochondrial function, spindle assembly and fertility. Human evidence is lacking.

mechanisms.name: Follicular fluid oxidative stress
mechanisms.description: Follicular fluid surrounds the maturing egg. Higher ROS, lipid peroxidation and 8-OHdG (oxidative DNA damage) in follicular fluid are associated with degenerate oocytes, fertilization failure and poor embryos. Obesity raises follicular insulin, triglycerides and CRP. These markers are research tools, not validated clinical tests.

mechanisms.name: Lipotoxicity in obesity
mechanisms.description: Excess lipid in the follicle leads to lipid accumulation in the oocyte, endoplasmic-reticulum stress, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and cumulus-cell apoptosis, lowering fertilization.

mechanisms.name: The egg repairs sperm DNA damage
mechanisms.description: Until the embryo's own genome switches on (4-8 cell stage), DNA repair relies on maternal transcripts and proteins stored in the egg. Good-quality eggs can partly compensate for sperm DNA fragmentation: in one cohort sperm DNA damage reduced pregnancy with patients' own eggs but not with donor eggs.

mechanisms.name: Folliculogenesis timeline (why 3 months)
mechanisms.description: A resting follicle takes several months to reach the preantral stage, then about 70-85 more days to grow to the selectable 2-5 mm stage and ovulate. The egg ovulated in a given month has therefore been developing in the follicular environment of the preceding ~3 months, which is the window lifestyle changes can influence.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Aponte-Mellado A, Premkumar BJ, et al.
references.title: The effects of oxidative stress on female reproduction: a review
references.finding: Narrative review: oxidative stress is implicated in endometriosis, PCOS, unexplained infertility and pregnancy complications; antioxidant evidence is mostly animal/in-vitro and conflicting.

references.authors: Shkolnik K, Tadmor A, Ben-Dor S, et al.
references.title: Reactive oxygen species are indispensable in ovulation
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: In mice, antioxidants injected into the ovarian bursa reduced ovulation and blocked LH-induced cumulus expansion; H2O2 mimicked LH. ROS are an essential pre-ovulatory signal.

references.authors: May-Panloup P, Boucret L, Chao de la Barca JM, et al.
references.title: Ovarian ageing: the role of mitochondria in oocytes and follicles
references.finding: Oocytes are the most mitochondria-rich cells in the body; ageing-related mtDNA instability and impaired mitochondrial biogenesis in oocytes and granulosa cells are closely linked to declining oocyte quality.

references.authors: Cree LM, Samuels DC, de Sousa Lopes SC, et al.
references.title: A reduction of mitochondrial DNA molecules during embryogenesis explains the rapid segregation of genotypes
references.finding: Mouse study: mtDNA is maternally inherited and passes through a genetic bottleneck (partitioning of mtDNA molecules during embryogenesis and germ-cell proliferation) that explains rapid shifts in heteroplasmy between generations.

references.authors: Franasiak JM, Forman EJ, Hong KH, et al.
references.title: The nature of aneuploidy with increasing age of the female partner: a review of 15,169 consecutive trophectoderm biopsies evaluated with comprehensive chromosomal screening
references.finding: Embryo aneuploidy was lowest at ages 26-30 and rose predictably after 26; the chance of having no euploid embryo was 2-6% at ages 26-37, 33% at 42 and 53% at 44.

references.authors: Gruhn JR, Zielinska AP, Shukla V, et al.
references.title: Chromosome errors in human eggs shape natural fertility over reproductive life span
references.finding: Aneuploidy in human eggs follows a U-curve with age; in older women it is driven by centromeric and more extensive loss of sister-chromatid cohesion.

references.authors: Bertoldo MJ, Listijono DR, Ho WJ, et al.
references.title: NAD(+) Repletion Rescues Female Fertility during Reproductive Aging
references.finding: In aged mice, oocyte NAD+ falls with age; the precursor NMN restored oocyte quality, fertility and embryo development. Mouse data only.

references.authors: Miao Y, Cui Z, Gao Q, et al.
references.title: Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Supplementation Reverses the Declining Quality of Maternally Aged Oocytes
references.finding: In naturally aged mice, NMN restored oocyte NAD+, spindle/chromosome structure, fertilization ability and mitochondrial function and lowered ROS. Mouse data only.

references.authors: Gougeon A
references.title: Dynamics of follicular growth in the human: a model from preliminary results
references.finding: Human follicle growth is very long: the ovulatory follicle comes from a cohort of preantral follicles that differentiated about 85 days earlier; it is recruited 15-20 days before ovulation.

references.authors: Gougeon A
references.title: Human ovarian follicular development: from activation of resting follicles to preovulatory maturation
references.finding: Several months are needed for a growing follicle to reach the preantral stage, then about 70 more days to reach 2 mm before cyclic selection.

references.authors: Das S, Chattopadhyay R, Ghosh S, et al.
references.title: Reactive oxygen species level in follicular fluid--embryo quality marker in IVF?
references.finding: Higher follicular fluid ROS and lipid peroxidation were associated with fertilization failure, pronuclear arrest and poor-grade embryos.

references.authors: Tamura H, Takasaki A, Miwa I, et al.
references.title: Oxidative stress impairs oocyte quality and melatonin protects oocytes from free radical damage and improves fertilization rate
references.finding: Follicular 8-OHdG (oxidative DNA damage) was higher where many oocytes degenerated; melatonin 3 mg/day and/or vitamin E 600 mg/day lowered follicular oxidative markers, and melatonin was associated with better fertilization vs the previous failed cycle (not randomized).

references.authors: Meseguer M, Santiso R, Garrido N, et al.
references.title: Effect of sperm DNA fragmentation on pregnancy outcome depends on oocyte quality
references.finding: Sperm DNA fragmentation lowered pregnancy odds when the woman's own (infertile-patient) oocytes were used, but had no significant effect with donor oocytes, implying good oocytes can compensate for sperm DNA damage.

references.authors: Ménézo Y, Dale B, Cohen M
references.title: DNA damage and repair in human oocytes and embryos: a review
references.finding: Early embryos rely on maternally stored DNA-repair transcripts until embryonic genome activation at the 4-8 cell stage; the oocyte must repair DNA damage brought in by sperm.

references.authors: ACOG Committee on Gynecologic Practice; ASRM Practice Committee
references.title: Female age-related fertility decline. Committee Opinion No. 589
references.finding: ACOG/ASRM: female fecundity declines gradually from about age 32 and more rapidly after 37; evaluate after 6 months of trying at >35 and immediately at >40.

references.authors: Murri M, Luque-Ramírez M, Insenser M, et al.
references.title: Circulating markers of oxidative stress and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS): a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Women with PCOS had higher circulating malondialdehyde (+47%), homocysteine (+23%) and ADMA, and about 50% lower glutathione, independent of weight excess.

references.authors: Teede HJ, Tay CT, Laven JJE, et al.
references.title: Recommendations From the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
references.finding: 2023 international PCOS guideline (77 evidence-based, 54 consensus recommendations): emphasizes healthy lifestyle and evidence-based medical and fertility therapy; evidence generally low-to-moderate quality.

references.authors: Sanchez AM, Vanni VS, Bartiromo L, et al.
references.title: Is the oocyte quality affected by endometriosis? A review of the literature
references.finding: Systematic review: oocytes from women with endometriosis are more likely to fail in-vitro maturation, show altered morphology and lower mitochondrial content; granulosa cells show more ROS.

references.authors: Hamdan M, Dunselman G, Li TC, et al.
references.title: The impact of endometrioma on IVF/ICSI outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Endometrioma was associated with fewer oocytes retrieved and more cancelled cycles, but similar live birth rates (OR 0.98); surgery before IVF did not improve outcomes.

references.authors: Wang Q, Ratchford AM, Chi MM, et al.
references.title: Maternal diabetes causes mitochondrial dysfunction and meiotic defects in murine oocytes
references.finding: In diabetic mice, oocytes showed abnormal mitochondrial structure and distribution, lower ATP and TCA metabolites, more spindle defects and higher aneuploidy.

references.authors: Whitworth KW, Baird DD, Stene LC, et al.
references.title: Fecundability among women with type 1 and type 2 diabetes in the Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort Study
references.finding: Fecundability odds were lower in women with type 1 diabetes (FOR 0.76) and type 2 diabetes (FOR 0.64), even with regular cycles.

references.authors: Robker RL, Akison LK, Bennett BD, et al.
references.title: Obese women exhibit differences in ovarian metabolites, hormones, and gene expression compared with moderate-weight women
references.finding: Higher BMI was associated with higher follicular fluid insulin, lactate, triglycerides and C-reactive protein: an altered, more inflammatory follicular environment.

references.authors: Wu LL, Dunning KR, Yang X, et al.
references.title: High-fat diet causes lipotoxicity responses in cumulus-oocyte complexes and decreased fertilization rates
references.finding: High-fat-diet obese mice had lipid-laden oocytes with reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, ER stress, cumulus apoptosis and lower fertilization; ER stress markers were also raised in granulosa cells of obese women.

references.authors: Sermondade N, Huberlant S, Bourhis-Lefebvre V, et al.
references.title: Female obesity is negatively associated with live birth rate following IVF: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Obese women (BMI >= 30) had lower live birth rates after IVF than normal-weight women (RR 0.85); worse when combined with PCOS.

references.authors: Kiddy DS, Hamilton-Fairley D, Bush A, et al.
references.title: Improvement in endocrine and ovarian function during dietary treatment of obese women with polycystic ovary syndrome
references.finding: Women who lost more than 5% of body weight on a 1000 kcal diet had lower insulin, higher SHBG and 9 of 11 improved reproductive function; those losing less than 5% did not improve.

references.authors: Mutsaerts MA, van Oers AM, Groen H, et al.
references.title: Randomized Trial of a Lifestyle Program in Obese Infertile Women
references.finding: LIFEstyle trial: a 6-month lifestyle program before fertility treatment (mean loss 4.4 kg) did not increase healthy term singleton births at 24 months (27.1% vs 35.2%; RR 0.77).

references.authors: Einarsson S, Bergh C, Friberg B, et al.
references.title: Weight reduction intervention for obese infertile women prior to IVF: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Intensive weight loss (12 weeks 880 kcal/day, mean -9.4 kg) before IVF did not change IVF live birth (29.6% vs 27.5%), but more spontaneous conceptions occurred (10.5% vs 2.6%).

references.authors: Best D, Avenell A, Bhattacharya S
references.title: How effective are weight-loss interventions for improving fertility in women and men who are overweight or obese? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the evidence
references.finding: In overweight/obese women, reduced-calorie diet and exercise interventions increased pregnancy (RR 1.59) and improved ovulation; miscarriage was not reduced.

references.authors: Augood C, Duckitt K, Templeton AA
references.title: Smoking and female infertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Female smokers had higher odds of infertility (OR 1.60) and lower odds of pregnancy per IVF cycle (OR 0.66).

references.authors: Waylen AL, Metwally M, Jones GL, et al.
references.title: Effects of cigarette smoking upon clinical outcomes of assisted reproduction: a meta-analysis
references.finding: Smokers undergoing ART had lower odds of live birth per cycle (OR 0.54) and clinical pregnancy (OR 0.56) and higher miscarriage (OR 2.65).

references.authors: Zhu D, Chung HF, Pandeya N, et al.
references.title: Relationships between intensity, duration, cumulative dose, and timing of smoking with age at menopause: A pooled analysis of individual data from 17 observational studies
references.finding: Current smokers had about twice the risk of premature (RRR 2.05) and early (1.80) menopause, with clear dose-response; women who had quit more than 10 years earlier had the same risk as never smokers.

references.authors: Freour T, Masson D, Mirallie S, et al.
references.title: Active smoking compromises IVF outcome and affects ovarian reserve
references.finding: Active smokers had lower AMH, fewer mature oocytes (8.6 vs 12.1) and lower clinical pregnancy (10% vs 29.6%) than non-smokers.

references.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
references.title: Tobacco or marijuana use and infertility: a committee opinion
references.finding: ASRM committee opinion reviewing deleterious effects of tobacco, nicotine and marijuana on conception, ovarian follicular dynamics, gamete mutations and ART outcomes, and smoking-cessation strategies.

references.authors: Fan D, Liu L, Xia Q, et al.
references.title: Female alcohol consumption and fecundability: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis
references.finding: Any alcohol use was associated with lower fecundability (RR 0.87); light (<=12.5 g/day) 0.89, moderate-heavy (>12.5 g/day) 0.77; per 12.5 g/day RR 0.98.

references.authors: Mikkelsen EM, Riis AH, Wise LA, et al.
references.title: Alcohol consumption and fecundability: prospective Danish cohort study
references.finding: Fewer than 14 servings/week had no discernible effect on fecundability; >=14 servings/week FR 0.82 (imprecise).

references.authors: Rossi BV, Berry KF, Hornstein MD, et al.
references.title: Effect of alcohol consumption on in vitro fertilization
references.finding: Women drinking >=4 drinks/week had 16% lower odds of IVF live birth (OR 0.84); 21% lower when both partners did.

references.authors: Abadia L, Chiu YH, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: The association between pre-treatment maternal alcohol and caffeine intake and outcomes of assisted reproduction in a prospectively followed cohort
references.finding: Low-to-moderate pre-treatment alcohol (<=12 g/day) and caffeine (<200 mg/day) were not associated with ART outcomes.

references.authors: Lyngsø J, Ramlau-Hansen CH, Bay B, et al.
references.title: Association between coffee or caffeine consumption and fecundity and fertility: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis
references.finding: Caffeine was associated with spontaneous abortion (RR 1.37 at 300 mg/day; 2.32 at 600 mg/day) but showed little or no association with fecundability or fertility-treatment outcomes.

references.authors: Wesselink AK, Wise LA, Rothman KJ, et al.
references.title: Caffeine and caffeinated beverage consumption and fecundability in a preconception cohort
references.finding: Female total caffeine intake was not associated with fecundability; male intake >=300 mg/day was (FR 0.72).

references.authors: Chen LW, Wu Y, Neelakantan N, et al.
references.title: Maternal caffeine intake during pregnancy and risk of pregnancy loss: a categorical and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies
references.finding: Caffeine in pregnancy: pregnancy-loss RR 1.02 at 50-149 mg/day, 1.16 at 150-349, 1.40 at 350-699, 1.72 at >=700; +7% per 100 mg/day.

references.authors: ASRM Practice Committee and SREI Practice Committee
references.title: Optimizing natural fertility: a committee opinion
references.finding: ASRM/SREI: >500 mg caffeine/day linked to lower fertility, 1-2 cups/day has no apparent effect; >2 drinks/day best avoided; folic acid >=400 ug/day; insufficient evidence that a specific diet improves natural fertility.

references.authors: Legro RS, Sauer MV, Mottla GL, et al.
references.title: Effect of air quality on assisted human reproduction
references.finding: Higher NO2 at home and at the IVF lab was associated with lower live birth (e.g. OR 0.76 per 0.01 ppm after embryo transfer); PM2.5 during culture was associated with lower conception.

references.authors: La Marca A, Spaggiari G, Domenici D, et al.
references.title: Elevated levels of nitrous dioxide are associated with lower AMH levels: a real-world analysis
references.finding: Higher NO2 (and weakly PM10/PM2.5) exposure was associated with lower AMH; NO2 remained associated after age adjustment.

references.authors: Gaskins AJ, Mínguez-Alarcón L, Fong KC, et al.
references.title: Supplemental Folate and the Relationship Between Traffic-Related Air Pollution and Livebirth Among Women Undergoing Assisted Reproduction
references.finding: Among women taking <800 ug/day supplemental folate, each 20 ppb NO2 was associated with 24% lower odds of live birth; no association at >=800 ug/day.

references.authors: Hauser R, Gaskins AJ, Souter I, et al.
references.title: Urinary Phthalate Metabolite Concentrations and Reproductive Outcomes among Women Undergoing in Vitro Fertilization: Results from the EARTH Study
references.finding: Highest vs lowest quartile of urinary DEHP metabolites: fewer oocytes and mature oocytes, and 19 percentage points lower clinical pregnancy and live birth per cycle.

references.authors: Mok-Lin E, Ehrlich S, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: Urinary bisphenol A concentrations and ovarian response among women undergoing IVF
references.finding: Each log-unit increase in urinary BPA was associated with 12% fewer oocytes retrieved and lower peak estradiol.

references.authors: Butts CD, Bloom MS, McGough A, et al.
references.title: Toxic elements in follicular fluid adversely influence the likelihood of pregnancy and live birth in women undergoing IVF
references.finding: Follicular fluid mercury above ~0.51 ug/L and higher lead were associated with lower live birth after IVF (Pb RR 0.68).

references.authors: Wallace WH, Thomson AB, Kelsey TW
references.title: The radiosensitivity of the human oocyte
references.finding: Modelling estimates the radiation dose that destroys half of human oocytes (LD50) at less than 2 Gy.

references.authors: Oktay K, Harvey BE, Partridge AH, et al.
references.title: Fertility Preservation in Patients With Cancer: ASCO Clinical Practice Guideline Update
references.finding: ASCO: discuss infertility risk before cancer treatment as early as possible; oocyte and embryo cryopreservation are standard; GnRH agonists are not a substitute for proven preservation methods.

references.authors: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, et al.
references.title: 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)
references.finding: IOC 2023 consensus on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport: low energy availability causes health effects including reproductive dysfunction, with a clinical assessment tool for diagnosis.

references.authors: Gudmundsdottir SL, Flanders WD, Augestad LB
references.title: Physical activity and fertility in women: the North-Trøndelag Health Study
references.finding: Women active on most days had 3.2-fold odds of fertility problems and exercising to exhaustion 2.3-fold, vs low activity; no association at lower activity levels.

references.authors: Wise LA, Rothman KJ, Mikkelsen EM, et al.
references.title: A prospective cohort study of physical activity and time to pregnancy
references.finding: Vigorous activity >=5 h/week vs none: fecundability ratio 0.68 (lean women); moderate activity >=5 h/week: 1.18; no harm from vigorous activity in women with BMI >=25.

references.authors: Gaskins AJ, Williams PL, Keller MG, et al.
references.title: Maternal physical and sedentary activities in relation to reproductive outcomes following IVF
references.finding: Pre-treatment moderate-to-vigorous activity (median 2.8 h/week) was not associated with IVF outcomes; some vigorous activities were associated with higher live birth.

references.authors: Mena GP, Mielke GI, Brown WJ
references.title: The effect of physical activity on reproductive health outcomes in young women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Physical-activity interventions increased pregnancy (RR 2.10) and live birth (RR 2.11) vs no therapy in women with reproductive problems (small number of trials).

references.authors: Stocker LJ, Macklon NS, Cheong YC, et al.
references.title: Influence of shift work on early reproductive outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Shift work was associated with menstrual disruption (aOR 1.15); infertility association was not robust after adjustment (aOR 1.11); night shifts were associated with early pregnancy loss (aOR 1.41).

references.authors: Willis SK, Hatch EE, Wesselink AK, et al.
references.title: Female sleep patterns, shift work, and fecundability in a North American preconception cohort study
references.finding: Trouble sleeping >50% of the time was associated with lower fecundability (FR 0.87); <6 h sleep FR 0.89 (imprecise); shift work was not associated.

references.authors: Lynch CD, Sundaram R, Maisog JM, et al.
references.title: Preconception stress increases the risk of infertility: results from a couple-based prospective cohort study--the LIFE study
references.finding: Highest vs lowest tertile of salivary alpha-amylase (stress marker) was associated with 29% lower fecundability and 2-fold infertility risk; cortisol was not associated.

references.authors: Boivin J, Griffiths E, Venetis CA
references.title: Emotional distress in infertile women and failure of assisted reproductive technologies: meta-analysis of prospective psychosocial studies
references.finding: Pre-treatment anxiety or depression was not associated with pregnancy after a cycle of ART.

references.authors: Karayiannis D, Kontogianni MD, Mendorou C, et al.
references.title: Adherence to the Mediterranean diet and IVF success rate among non-obese women attempting fertility
references.finding: Lowest vs highest tertile of Mediterranean diet score had lower live birth (26.6% vs 48.8%; adjusted RR 0.32); association seen only in women under 35; no effect on oocyte or embryo measures.

references.authors: Gaskins AJ, Nassan FL, Chiu YH, et al.
references.title: Dietary patterns and outcomes of assisted reproduction
references.finding: The profertility diet was associated with 53% higher odds of live birth per SD; top vs bottom quartile +28 percentage points; not related to oocyte counts. Mediterranean diet benefit plateaued after the second quartile.

references.authors: Vujkovic M, de Vries JH, Lindemans J, et al.
references.title: The preconception Mediterranean dietary pattern in couples undergoing in vitro fertilization/intracytoplasmic sperm injection treatment increases the chance of pregnancy
references.finding: High couple adherence to a Mediterranean dietary pattern was associated with higher pregnancy odds after IVF/ICSI (OR 1.4) and higher folate and vitamin B6 in blood and follicular fluid.

references.authors: Muffone ARMC, de Oliveira Lübke PDP, Rabito EI
references.title: Mediterranean diet and infertility: a systematic review with meta-analysis of cohort studies
references.finding: Pooled evidence linking Mediterranean diet adherence to live birth and pregnancy was inconsistent and insufficient to support clinical application.

references.authors: Gaskins AJ, Chavarro JE
references.title: Diet and fertility: a review
references.finding: Review: supplemental folic acid (above neural-tube-defect doses) is consistently associated with better fertility; antioxidant supplements do not help women in fertility treatment; omega-3s appear beneficial; vitamin D matters mainly in deficiency.

references.authors: Chavarro JE, Rich-Edwards JW, Rosner BA, et al.
references.title: Diet and lifestyle in the prevention of ovulatory disorder infertility
references.finding: Highest vs lowest quintile of a 'fertility diet' score was associated with 66% lower risk of ovulatory infertility (RR 0.34); five or more low-risk lifestyle factors with 69% lower risk.

references.authors: Gaskins AJ, Afeiche MC, Wright DL, et al.
references.title: Dietary folate and reproductive success among women undergoing assisted reproduction
references.finding: Supplemental folate >800 ug/day vs <400 ug/day was associated with a 20 percentage-point higher live birth rate after ART.

references.authors: Cueto HT, Riis AH, Hatch EE, et al.
references.title: Folic acid supplementation and fecundability: a Danish prospective cohort study
references.finding: Folic acid or multivitamin supplementation was associated with higher fecundability (FR 1.15), more so with irregular cycles.

references.authors: US Preventive Services Task Force
references.title: Folic Acid Supplementation to Prevent Neural Tube Defects: US Preventive Services Task Force Reaffirmation Recommendation Statement
references.finding: USPSTF: everyone planning or capable of pregnancy should take a daily supplement containing 0.4-0.8 mg (400-800 ug) folic acid (A recommendation).

references.authors: Chu J, Gallos I, Tobias A, et al.
references.title: Vitamin D and assisted reproductive treatment outcome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Vitamin D-replete women undergoing ART had higher live birth than deficient/insufficient women (OR 1.33); no association with miscarriage.

references.authors: Zhou X, Wu X, Luo X, et al.
references.title: Effect of Vitamin D Supplementation on In Vitro Fertilization Outcomes: A Trial Sequential Meta-Analysis of 5 Randomized Controlled Trials
references.finding: In vitamin D-deficient infertile women, supplementation raised chemical pregnancy (RR 1.53) but not clinical pregnancy (RR 1.34, NS) or embryo quality.

references.authors: Chiu YH, Karmon AE, Gaskins AJ, et al.
references.title: Serum omega-3 fatty acids and treatment outcomes among women undergoing assisted reproduction
references.finding: Each 1% higher serum long-chain omega-3 was associated with 8% higher probability of live birth after ART.

references.authors: Nehra D, Le HD, Fallon EM, et al.
references.title: Prolonging the female reproductive lifespan and improving egg quality with dietary omega-3 fatty acids
references.finding: In mice, omega-3-rich diets prolonged reproductive function and improved oocyte quality at advanced maternal age; omega-6-rich diets worsened it.

references.authors: Showell MG, Mackenzie-Proctor R, Jordan V, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants for female subfertility
references.finding: Very low-quality evidence: antioxidants might raise live birth (OR 1.81) but evidence is unreliable; 2026 editorial note: 7 included trials since retracted and 2 under expression of concern (conclusions retained).

references.authors: Xu Y, Nisenblat V, Lu C, et al.
references.title: Pretreatment with coenzyme Q10 improves ovarian response and embryo quality in low-prognosis young women with decreased ovarian reserve: a randomized controlled trial
references.n: 186 women <35 with poor ovarian reserve (169 analysed)
references.finding: CoQ10 600 mg/day (200 mg three times daily) for 60 days before IVF increased oocytes retrieved (median 4 vs 2), fertilization and good embryos; live birth 29% vs 16% was not statistically significant.

references.authors: Ben-Meir A, Burstein E, Borrego-Alvarez A, et al.
references.title: Coenzyme Q10 restores oocyte mitochondrial function and fertility during reproductive aging
references.finding: Oocyte ageing in mice and humans involves reduced CoQ-synthesis enzymes and lower ATP; CoQ10 reversed age-related oocyte deficits in mice.

references.authors: Florou P, Anagnostis P, Theocharis P, et al.
references.title: Does coenzyme Q(10) supplementation improve fertility outcomes in women undergoing assisted reproductive technology procedures? A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized-controlled trials
references.finding: CoQ10 increased clinical pregnancy (28.8% vs 14.1%; OR 2.44) but not live birth (OR 1.67, NS) or miscarriage.

references.authors: Zhang Y, Zhang C, Shu J, et al.
references.title: Adjuvant treatment strategies in ovarian stimulation for poor responders undergoing IVF: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
references.finding: In poor responders, DHEA (OR 2.46) and CoQ10 (OR 2.22) were associated with higher clinical pregnancy vs control; CoQ10 had the lowest cancellation rate.

references.authors: Hu KL, Ye X, Wang S, et al.
references.title: Melatonin Application in Assisted Reproductive Technology: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials
references.finding: Melatonin increased clinical pregnancy (OR 1.43) and oocyte/embryo counts but not live birth (OR 1.38, 3 RCTs, NS); low-quality evidence.

references.authors: Fernando S, Wallace EM, Rombauts L, et al.
references.title: The effect of melatonin on ultrasound markers of follicular development: A double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial
references.journal: Aust N Z J Obstet Gynaecol
references.finding: Melatonin 2, 4 or 8 mg twice daily during IVF stimulation did not change follicle number or ovarian vascular indices vs placebo (pilot).

references.authors: Showell MG, Mackenzie-Proctor R, Jordan V, et al.
references.title: Inositol for subfertile women with polycystic ovary syndrome
references.finding: Very low-quality evidence; uncertain whether myo-inositol improves live birth (OR 2.42, 95% CI 0.75-7.83) or clinical pregnancy in PCOS before IVF.

references.authors: Fitz V, Graca S, Mahalingaiah S, et al.
references.title: Inositol for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis to Inform the 2023 Update of the International Evidence-based PCOS Guidelines
references.finding: For the 2023 PCOS guideline: inositol evidence is limited and inconclusive; possible metabolic benefits; little difference from metformin for reproductive outcomes.

references.authors: Pacchiarotti A, Carlomagno G, Antonini G, et al.
references.title: Effect of myo-inositol and melatonin versus myo-inositol, in a randomized controlled trial, for improving in vitro fertilization of patients with polycystic ovarian syndrome
references.finding: RETRACTED (2026). Claimed myo-inositol 4 g + folic acid 400 ug + melatonin 3 mg improved oocyte and embryo quality; should not be relied on.

references.authors: Thakker D, Raval A, Patel I, et al.
references.title: N-acetylcysteine for polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled clinical trials
references.finding: NAC improved ovulation and pregnancy vs placebo but was inferior to metformin; trials had high risk of bias.

references.authors: Rizk AY, Bedaiwy MA, Al-Inany HG
references.title: N-acetyl-cysteine is a novel adjuvant to clomiphene citrate in clomiphene citrate-resistant patients with polycystic ovary syndrome
references.finding: NAC 1.2 g/day added to clomiphene raised ovulation (49.3% vs 1.3%) and pregnancy (21.3% vs 0%) vs placebo.

references.authors: Naik S, Lepine S, Nagels HE, et al.
references.title: Androgens (dehydroepiandrosterone or testosterone) for women undergoing assisted reproduction
references.finding: Cochrane: DHEA probably makes little or no difference to live birth in poor responders (OR 1.30, NS, moderate certainty); testosterone probably improves it (OR 2.53).

references.authors: Wiser A, Gonen O, Ghetler Y, et al.
references.title: Addition of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) for poor-responder patients before and during IVF treatment improves the pregnancy rate: a randomized prospective study
references.finding: DHEA 75 mg/day before and during IVF was associated with higher live birth (23.1% vs 4.0%) in a very small trial.

references.authors: Ismail AM, Hamed AH, Saso S, et al.
references.title: Adding L-carnitine to clomiphene resistant PCOS women improves the quality of ovulation and the pregnancy rate. A randomized clinical trial
references.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
references.finding: RETRACTED. Claimed L-carnitine 3 g/day with clomiphene raised pregnancy from 5.8% to 51.5%; should not be relied on.

references.authors: Ochiai A, Kuroda K
references.title: Preconception resveratrol intake against infertility: Friend or foe?
references.finding: Resveratrol may support ovarian function via SIRT1 but suppresses endometrial decidualization (anti-deciduogenic) and its teratogenicity is unknown; avoid in the luteal phase and pregnancy.

references.authors: Ochiai A, Kuroda K, Ikemoto Y, et al.
references.title: Influence of resveratrol supplementation on IVF-embryo transfer cycle outcomes
references.finding: Resveratrol 200 mg/day during embryo-transfer cycles was associated with lower clinical pregnancy (OR 0.54) and higher miscarriage (OR 2.60).

references.authors: Ardehjani NA, Agha-Hosseini M, Nashtaei MS, et al.
references.title: Resveratrol ameliorates mitochondrial biogenesis and reproductive outcomes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome undergoing assisted reproduction: a randomized, triple-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial
references.finding: Resveratrol 800 mg/day for 60 days lowered follicular fluid oxidative stress and raised oocyte maturity and good-quality embryos, but pregnancy rates did not differ.

references.authors: Di Tucci C, Galati G, Mattei G, et al.
references.title: The role of alpha lipoic acid in female and male infertility: a systematic review
references.finding: Systematic review (28 articles): alpha-lipoic acid shows some positive effects on oocyte maturation, embryo grade and endometriosis pain, but clinical evidence is limited and more trials are needed.

references.authors: ESHRE Add-ons working group; Lundin K, Bentzen JG, et al.
references.title: Good practice recommendations on add-ons in reproductive medicine†
references.finding: ESHRE add-ons recommendations: antioxidant therapy lacks reliable evidence of higher live birth and is not recommended in ART; routine adjuncts (GH, DHEA, testosterone, metformin) are not supported.

references.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Ovarian Stimulation; Bosch E, Broer S, et al.
references.title: ESHRE guideline: ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI(†)
references.finding: ESHRE ovarian stimulation guideline: hormone pre-treatment and adjuvants (metformin, growth hormone, testosterone, DHEA, aspirin, sildenafil) are not recommended for improving efficacy.

references.authors: Dechanet C, Anahory T, Mathieu Daude JC, et al.
references.title: Effects of cigarette smoking on reproduction
references.finding: Systematic review: cigarette smoke contains thousands of toxicants (nicotine, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, cadmium) that target folliculogenesis, steroidogenesis and every other reproductive stage, dose-dependently.

references.authors: Hahn KA, Wise LA, Rothman KJ, et al.
references.title: Caffeine and caffeinated beverage consumption and risk of spontaneous abortion
references.finding: Preconception caffeine was not associated with miscarriage (HR 1.09 for >=300 vs <100 mg/day), whereas early-pregnancy intake of 100-299 mg/day was (HR ~1.5-1.6).

references.authors: Lim SS, Hutchison SK, Van Ryswyk E, et al.
references.title: Lifestyle changes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
references.finding: Cochrane: lifestyle interventions in PCOS may modestly reduce weight and free androgen index; no trial reported live birth or miscarriage.

references.authors: Szymanska KJ, Tan X, Oktay K
references.title: Unraveling the mechanisms of chemotherapy-induced damage to human primordial follicle reserve: road to developing therapeutics for fertility preservation and reversing ovarian aging
references.finding: Gonadotoxic chemotherapy (e.g. cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin) induces DNA double-strand breaks and apoptosis of primordial-follicle oocytes within 12-24 h, plus stromal and microvascular damage.

references.authors: Fernando S, Biggs SN, Horne RSC, et al.
references.title: The impact of melatonin on the sleep patterns of women undergoing IVF: a double blind RCT
references.finding: Melatonin 2, 4 or 8 mg twice daily from cycle day 2 to egg retrieval did not cause daytime sleepiness or change objective sleep vs placebo.
